svg.aria-label: What each front end requires you to install in each cluster of a fleet, and what an attacker who compromises an agent pod actually reaches. flint-lite installs nothing in consumer clusters but concentrates one hub; flint-lean and flint-passthrough install a CSI driver and broker in every cluster and meet in the bucket.
svg.text: flint-lite — one hub, N clusters
flint-lean — N syncers, one bucket
flint-passthrough — N mounts, one bucket
the HUB cluster — install here, once per project
· flint-lite-operator (or the chart, one release per hub)
· the hub Deployment, Service, ConfigMap and PVC it renders
· optionally flint-hub-gateway — one door for the whole fleet,
holding ONE credential instead of one per hub
This cluster is now a dependency of every other one.
It holds the only copy of the live tree that is not in S3.
every CONSUMER cluster — install NOTHING
The data path is the node's own kernel NFS client. There is no
driver, no DaemonSet, no CRD and no flint image anywhere.
At most a PV and PVC — or the stock nfs-subdir provisioner,
which mints directories and never carries a byte.
This is the cheapest fleet onboarding of the three, by far.
what it costs you
One pod is the coherence authority, so one pod is also the
single point of failure and the NIC ceiling for the project.
A hard NFS mount against a suspended hub HANGS — nothing in
the data path wakes a share, so something must write the
wake annotation before an address is handed to anyone.
EVERY cluster — install the same three things
· flint-s3-csi — the node DaemonSet, the workers namespace
and its admission policy
· flint-s3-broker — one per cluster, because TokenReview runs
against the LOCAL API server
· flint-lean — the CRD plus a thin controller (claim stamping,
bucket posture, the MPU sweep)
and no cluster depends on any other
The clusters never talk. They meet in the bucket, and the
arbitration that keeps them honest lives there too — a CAS
on the subtree lease, which no cluster can route around.
So the single-writer rule holds ACROSS clusters, which is
the one guarantee flint-lite's admission check cannot make.
what it costs you
A per-cluster install that must be kept in version step, and
a broker per cluster to configure and watch.
A lean volume still mounts with its controller absent — the
syncer claims the lease itself — so the controller is an
operability component, not a data-path one.
EVERY cluster — install two things
· flint-s3-csi — the same node DaemonSet and broker as lean;
one install serves both front ends
· flint-passthrough — the CRD, and nothing else. There is no
workload in that chart and no controller behind the CR.
Nothing about a passthrough mount converges, so there is
nothing to reconcile and no status to read.
the fleet story is: there isn't one
Pods in twenty clusters can mount one prefix and none of
them coordinates, because none of them has anything to
coordinate. S3 is already a multi-cluster service.
Scaling out is free precisely because nothing is shared
except the objects themselves.
what it costs you
Everything the other two provide. No POSIX, no rename, no
boundary, no manifest, no single-writer rule.
Two pods writing one key race, and the loser's write is
simply gone — with no cell anywhere recording that it
happened, because there is no control namespace.
S3 — the one thing every cluster, every front end and every fleet shape has in common. It is where the data lives; everything above is a way of reaching it.
Blast radius — an attacker owns one agent pod. What do they now have?
Assume the agent container is fully compromised and holds the user's token. This is the question the token cannot answer, because storage never sees it.
flint-lite — the whole share
The pod already has the mount. AUTH_SYS means it asserts its
own uid, and the default POSIX check LOGS rather than refuses —
so it reads and writes every file in the share, as anyone.
It cannot reach the BUCKET: the hub holds that credential and
the pod has none. That much is genuinely contained.
It can reach any other hub its network can route to, and the
next hub cannot tell it apart from a legitimate client.
Containment = one hub per project + a real network boundary.
Everything sharing a hub shares a fate. Size hubs accordingly.
flint-lean — the workspace, not the bucket
The pod has the tree it was already working in. It holds no S3
credential — the worker does, in another namespace, behind a
loopback door the agent container cannot reach.
So the attacker gets the files, and gets them published under
the workspace's own prefix. They do not get the bucket, other
workspaces, or a credential that outlives the pod.
The honest ceiling: writes are refused at the CONTROL plane,
not fenced on the data plane. A deposed syncer's writes land
as UNCITED versions — no coherent reader resolves them, but a
raw-key reader can still see them. A chosen ceiling, not a gap.
flint-passthrough — the prefix, as mounted
The pod has the mount, so it has whatever the mount has: the
prefix in the CR, at the CR's readOnly setting. Nothing more —
the keys are short-lived, scoped, and never in the pod's env.
This is the tightest of the three, and it is tight for a dull
reason: there is nothing else there to take.
Scope the CR, and you have scoped the breach. `readOnly: true`
is a real control here, not advice — the mount cannot write.
The residual risk is the one uid: every process in the pod
shares the mount, so pod-level isolation is user-level isolation.
